formationLabel: Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish established in 1915 · Parkside church cornerstone laid 1917 and church completed 1918 · merged into distinct successor June 8, 2003
currentUse: St. Casimir Parish ended as a separate institution when it merged with St. Peter on June 8, 2003 to form the distinct St. Peter and St. Casimir Parish. The successor retained the former St. Peter church on State Street, not the former St. Casimir church at 38 Parkside Avenue. Municipal records place the Parkside property under Westfield Public Schools control before transfer to the city in 2025, and a 2025 city sale notice scheduled on-site meetings there. These records support a standing former church/property under municipal disposition, not continued Catholic worship or current Lithuanian ministry.
summary: St. Casimir was Westfield's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish, established in 1915. Its church at 38 Parkside Avenue reached the cornerstone stage in 1917 and was completed in 1918. On June 8, 2003, St. Casimir and the distinct Slovak St. Peter Parish merged into a new successor, St. Peter and St. Casimir Parish. The successor retained St. Peter's State Street church, while Lithuanian objects from St. Casimir were preserved in the successor's worship space. The former Parkside property later passed through municipal-school control and was offered for sale by the city in 2025; it was not the successor's active church.

historicalNarrative.text: Westfield's Lithuanian Catholics organized St. Casimir Parish as an institution distinct from the city's Slovak St. Peter Parish. A local centennial account dates St. Casimir's establishment to 1915. The two ethnic parishes shared Catholic jurisdiction but retained separate institutional and building histories until 2003.

The local account places the St. Casimir cornerstone in 1917, while the diocesan outlet says the Lithuanian church at 38 Parkside Avenue was constructed in 1918. These are successive building milestones rather than competing parish-foundation dates. The Parkside church remained St. Casimir's worship site until the 2003 merger.

On June 8, 2003, St. Casimir closed its own doors and merged with St. Peter to form the distinct St. Peter and St. Casimir Parish. The successor retained St. Peter's State Street church rather than the Parkside building. Lithuanian religious objects were carried into the successor's worship setting, preserving material continuity without erasing the institutional merger.

The former St. Casimir property followed a separate post-parish course. A 2025 City Council agenda describes the former church at 38 Parkside Avenue and an adjacent Casimir Street lot as moving from Westfield Public Schools' care, custody, management, and control to the city. A later city sale notice used the name Parkside Academy and scheduled on-site meetings at 38 Parkside Avenue, supporting a standing-building reading while leaving its interior condition and post-sale disposition unresolved.

historicalNarrative.text: The Diocese of Springfield currently lists St. Peter and St. Casimir Parish with regular Masses at 32 State Street. The 2017 diocesan history names 24 State Street as the retained former St. Peter church. Current successor life is therefore established, while the address-number difference and the former Parkside property's later ownership remain separate unresolved property questions.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The 1915 establishment, 1917 cornerstone, and 1918 construction readings refer to different institutional and building milestones. St. Casimir's 2003 end was a merger into a distinct successor, not continued identity under a combined name. The retained successor site is the former St. Peter church; 24 State Street appears in the diocesan history, while the current diocesan directory lists 32 State Street.
gaps: The exact canonical erection and merger instruments; any worship location before the Parkside church; the precise 24/32 State Street address convention; sacramental-record custody; cemetery relationships; the terms and result of the 2025 Parkside sale process; current ownership; and the former church's interior condition remain unresolved. Current successor evidence does not establish present Lithuanian-language worship.
